episodes.title: Promote Primary & Secondary Domain Controller
episodes.subtitle: DC01 + DC02 / Active Directory
episodes.description: Promote the primary and secondary domain controllers on Windows Server, place them on their own network segment, verify the domain's health, and keep a record of the build.

chapters.label: Plan the build
chapters.title: Give every system a purpose
chapters.description: Understand Active Directory and where the controllers live before choosing names, addresses, and the starting configuration.
chapters.network: DC01 and DC02 are planned on VLAN 10, their own segment. The connections show where identity services will take shape.

chapters.label: Configure DC01
chapters.title: Create the first service point
chapters.description: Create the forest and bring Active Directory Domain Services online on DC01.
chapters.network: DC01 is configured. DC02 remains a planned system until it joins this same domain.

chapters.label: Bring in DC02
chapters.title: Give the domain a second home
chapters.description: Add a second writable controller and understand the availability it provides.
chapters.network: Both controllers serve the domain. The moving connection follows directory replication.

chapters.label: Verify the domain
chapters.title: Check the domain's health
chapters.description: Run DCDiag against each controller, confirm replication in both directions, and check each controller's roles and host firewall.
chapters.network: Select either controller below to follow a health check from the administration viewpoint.

chapters.label: Keep evidence
chapters.title: Leave a build you can explain
chapters.description: Record the configuration, observed results, and follow-up work in your training companion.
chapters.network: The directory now has two service points. Your build record connects choices with evidence.

episodes.outcomeSummary: One domain. Two writable controllers on their own segment. Replication and health checks you can explain and verify.
outcomes: Understand Active Directory
Promote both controllers
Verify and keep evidence

courses.title: Risk Management Framework
courses.subtitle: Scope, categorization, and control selection
courses.description: Apply the Risk Management Framework (RMF) to the system built in Inside the Network. Establish responsibilities and boundaries, justify mission impacts, and select a defensible control set before developing its Body of Evidence.
outcomes: Explain the RMF lifecycle and authorization responsibilities.
Define and categorize the Inside the Network practice system.
Select and tailor controls with documented ownership and rationale.

stages.title: RMF and authorization fundamentals
stages.detail: Explain the relationship between the RMF lifecycle, the Body of Evidence, the authorization package, and the authorization decision.

stages.title: Prepare and define the system
stages.detail: Establish what is being authorized, why it exists, and which organizational and system preparation decisions must be made before documentation expands.

stages.title: Categorize information and impacts
stages.detail: Justify confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts using information types and mission consequences. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

stages.title: Select and tailor controls
stages.detail: Translate the approved categorization and applicable requirements into a justified, assignable control set. Distinguish the control catalog from a selected baseline.

courses.outcomeSummary: A defined system, a justified categorization, and a control set with an owner and a reason for every choice.

courses.title: Body of Evidence
courses.subtitle: Document, demonstrate, and assess the network
courses.description: Develop the Body of Evidence for the same Inside the Network build. Write the System Security Plan, connect implementation to proof, organize evidence, and assess findings and residual risk for authorization review.
outcomes: Write specific implementation statements for the practice system.
Organize traceable, current technical and operational evidence.
Assess selected objectives and document findings, risk, and corrective actions.

stages.title: Write the system security plan
stages.detail: Write a System Security Plan (SSP) that describes the actual system and explains how selected controls are implemented.

stages.title: Connect implementation to proof
stages.detail: Collect technical and operational evidence that addresses the selected requirement and can support an assessment.

stages.title: Organize the Body of Evidence
stages.detail: Make evidence easy to retrieve, trace, and maintain across system changes and assessment cycles.

stages.title: Plan and perform assessment
stages.detail: Turn implementation claims into assessable objectives and distinguish a planned test from an observed result.

stages.title: Manage findings and residual risk
stages.detail: Translate weaknesses into mission-relevant risk and an accountable response. Explain the difference between technical severity and contextual risk.

relatedResources.title: Open the Body of Evidence workspace
relatedResources.detail: Ten examples with editable Markdown and CSV starters

courses.outcomeSummary: Implementation, assessment, and evidence organized so a reviewer can trace every control to proof.

courses.title: Authorization to Operate
courses.subtitle: Assemble, brief, and maintain the authorization package
courses.description: Turn the network’s Body of Evidence into a reviewable Authorization to Operate (ATO) package. Assemble the submission, brief the Authorizing Official on supported conclusions and remaining risk, and maintain evidence after the decision. Complete the shared course with the package capstone.
outcomes: Assemble a consistent authorization package for the practice system.
Present supported conclusions and residual risk for the Authorizing Official’s decision.
Complete the package capstone and plan ongoing monitoring.

stages.title: Assemble the authorization package
stages.detail: Build a reviewable package whose claims, assessment results, and open risks agree across documents.

stages.title: Present the authorization decision
stages.detail: Communicate mission need, the assessed security posture, unresolved risk, and proposed risk responses to the decision maker.

stages.title: Monitor and maintain authorization
stages.detail: Keep the authorization evidence useful as the system, threats, personnel, and dependencies change.

relatedResources.title: Open the authorization package capstone
relatedResources.detail: Four hour exercise · Assemble, defend, and maintain the practice package

relatedResources.title: Open the package manifest
relatedResources.detail: Organize the evidence and submission records

courses.outcomeSummary: A complete package, an honest risk picture, and a decision the authorizing official can defend.

stages.title: Map names to the network
stages.detail: DNS tells every domain member where its domain controllers are. Learn what it answers, set each controller's DNS client order, and record which server owns each name and how a client finds it.

stages.title: Configure forward and reverse zones
stages.detail: Forward lookup answers where a name lives. Reverse lookup answers which name is assigned to an address. AD integration lets the directory replicate zone data between the selected DNS servers.

stages.title: Create and maintain service records
stages.detail: Build a small, intentional record set. A host record identifies a machine; an alias provides a stable service name without making that alias a separate server.

stages.title: Prove resolution and directory discovery
stages.detail: Test each server explicitly before testing client fallback, then optionally watch a locator query on the wire. A correct DNS answer proves neither a sign-in nor access to a resource.

stages.title: Make SBD-DC01 the domain's time source
stages.detail: Kerberos tolerates minutes of skew, not more, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Make the PDC emulator the domain's reliable time source and let the domain hierarchy carry its time to everything else.

stages.title: Find the fault and record the fix
stages.detail: Troubleshoot one layer at a time: client settings, server reachability, authoritative data, replication, and finally the application that uses the name — or, for a sign-in failure, the clock.

courses.title: Configure DNS and time
courses.subtitle: Service discovery, zones, records, domain time & troubleshooting
courses.description: Learn how DNS lets every domain member find its domain controllers, then build dependable internal name resolution and time on DC01 and DC02: set each controller's DNS order, configure forward and reverse zones, manage service records, make the PDC emulator the domain's time source, and prove both in the air-gapped training network.
outcomes: Explain how DNS lets members find domain controllers, and plan internal DNS and client settings.
Configure secure AD-integrated zones and maintain records.
Test both resolvers, directory discovery, and client fallback.
Make the PDC emulator the domain's time source and verify the time hierarchy end to end.
courses.outcomeSummary: Names that resolve from either controller. A clock the whole domain trusts. Both proven, not assumed.

stages.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
stages.detail: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.

stages.title: Configure the offline Root CA
stages.detail: Treat root installation as a controlled event. Its private key is the highest-value secret in the hierarchy, and its configuration shapes the subordinate certificate it will sign.

stages.title: Create the issuing CA request
stages.detail: Prepare the online issuing server, but keep issuance paused until its CA certificate has been signed and installed. The request carries the public key; the private key stays protected on the issuing system or its approved key provider.

stages.title: Sign through the offline ceremony
stages.detail: A signing ceremony connects an approved request to an approved CA identity. A matching filename alone is not proof that the root should trust the request.

stages.title: Activate the issuing CA and distribute trust
stages.detail: A signed certificate is not yet a working CA. Install it, start Certificate Services, set the AIA and CDP locations every issued certificate will carry, and distribute the approved root through managed domain policy.

stages.title: Build the pki.sbd.test publication site
stages.detail: Every certificate the issuing CA has signed carries the pki.sbd.test URLs inside it. This lesson gives those URLs a real home: a small web site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 serving certificates and revocation lists to the whole network.

stages.title: Publish the trust data at its advertised URLs
stages.detail: A publication site is only correct when the filenames it serves match the URLs the certificates already carry. Copy the current certificates and CRLs into place, wire the issuing CA to keep them fresh, and prove retrieval from a client that has never cached anything.

stages.title: Separate template administration
stages.detail: Certificate templates are directory objects, and whoever edits them decides what the PKI will sign. Give that power its own seat — SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — with named administrators, instead of leaving it wherever a CA console happens to be open.

stages.title: Publish the first working templates
stages.detail: The default template set is a menu, not a deployment. Duplicate the two templates this network actually needs — computer authentication and server authentication — set their cryptography deliberately, and publish only those.

stages.title: Validate enrollment, revocation, and recovery
stages.detail: Finish from a clean domain client the way a relying system sees it: a pilot machine enrolls on its own, validates against the live publication site, and rejects a certificate you revoke — then the change-triggered scans record what this course did.

courses.title: Configure the two-tier PKI
courses.subtitle: Offline root, issuing CA, pki.sbd.test publication & templates
courses.description: Build a complete two-tier public key infrastructure: an offline standalone Root CA and an enterprise issuing CA, signed through a controlled ceremony, with trust data served from pki.sbd.test at the exact embedded URLs, template administration on its own seat, and enrollment and revocation proven end to end.
outcomes: Design the CA hierarchy and its publication dependencies.
Configure the offline root and sign an issuing CA request through controlled media transfer.
Publish certificates and CRLs at the exact URLs issued certificates carry, from pki.sbd.test.
Move template administration to a delegated seat and prove autoenrollment and revocation end to end.
courses.outcomeSummary: An offline root, a working issuing CA, and trust data served at exactly the URLs every certificate carries.

stages.title: Design and build the OU structure
stages.detail: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.

stages.title: Stage the tooling across the air gap
stages.detail: The hardening content is downloaded artifacts: the DISA Group Policy object (GPO) package, the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC), and STIG Viewer. They cross the boundary the way everything does here — reviewed, hashed, and carried on approved removable media.

stages.title: Capture the pre-hardening baseline
stages.detail: Measure before you change. A scan of the freshly built controllers shows the honest starting point, teaches what the operating system already secures by default, and becomes the before picture every later scan is compared against.

stages.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
stages.detail: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package into the central store, link by organizational unit, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.

stages.title: Rescan, reconcile, and record
stages.detail: The second scan is the verdict. Compare it with the baseline, let the automated results fill the checklists, and give every remaining open item a human answer.

stages.title: Set the rescan cadence and exception record
stages.detail: Hardening is a state you maintain, not a step you finish. Close the course by deciding who rescans, when, and which event forces an early look.

courses.title: Harden the baseline
courses.subtitle: OU design, DISA GPOs & STIG/SCAP verification
courses.description: Design the organizational unit structure, apply the DISA STIG Group Policy package to the verified network core, and prove the result with before-and-after SCAP scans, reconciled checklists, and a documented exception record.
outcomes: Design OUs for delegation and policy targeting, and redirect the default containers.
Import the DISA GPO package and link STIG policies by organizational unit.
Verify hardening with baseline and rescan SCAP results, reconciled checklists, and documented exceptions.
courses.outcomeSummary: An OU design built for delegation. DISA settings applied, scanned, and every exception written down.

courses.title: Addressing and tiered administration
courses.subtitle: DHCP, admin seats & where privilege may sign in
courses.description: Build the control plane before the fleet: DHCP with its core relay for the workstation VLAN, three dedicated administration systems in VLAN 60, and directory-enforced tier restrictions proven by both successful in-tier sessions and logged out-of-tier denials.
outcomes: Serve the workstation VLAN through an authorized DHCP server and core relay.
Stand up single-purpose administration hosts for each tier in the Admin OU.
Enforce and prove per-tier sign-in restrictions with captured denial evidence.

stages.title: Design the tiers and the address plan
stages.detail: Tiering is one sentence with teeth: credentials that control a tier never touch a less-trusted one. Write that policy against the OU structure, then plan the DHCP scope the fleet will live in — both before any host is built.

stages.title: Build SBD-DHCP01 and the relay
stages.detail: Addressing is the first service fifty machines will ask for. Build the DHCP server, authorize it in the directory so rogue servers stand out, and relay VLAN 80's broadcasts through the core.

stages.title: Build the administration systems
stages.detail: Privileged work gets dedicated, hardened seats: one jump host for Tier 0, one workstation for server administration, one for endpoint administration — each in the Admin OU, each doing nothing else.

stages.title: Restrict where privilege can sign in
stages.detail: The tier rule becomes real when the directory refuses the wrong sign-in. Give Tier 0 servers their own OU first, deny privileged logons on lower tiers by policy, protect the highest accounts, and make the refusal something you can show in a log.

stages.title: Prove the tiers and the addressing
stages.detail: Run the matrix: every tier's administration works from its seat, every cross-tier attempt fails with an event, and the addressing service behaves exactly as registered.

stages.title: Delta scan and hand off
stages.detail: Four new systems joined and the directory's logon policy changed — the cadence fires again. Baseline the newcomers, rescan what changed, and hand the next course a network that can finally be watched from somewhere safe.

courses.outcomeSummary: Addresses handed out on purpose, and privileged sessions that only ever start from the right seat.

courses.title: See everything: the logging pipeline
courses.subtitle: Collect, protect & analyze before the fleet arrives
courses.description: Build the model's collect → protect → analyze chain: Windows Event Forwarding and router syslog into SBD-SYSLOG01, hashed archives under a no-delete rule on SBD-AUDIT01, and working searches with one owned alert on SBD-SPLUNK01 — proven by a single event traced end to end.
outcomes: Forward the DC, admin-plane, and router-deny records into one collector by subscription.
Protect the archive with hash catalogs, named readers, and delete-by-process-only.
Prove the chain by tracing one event from source to analyst, with an owned alert.

stages.title: Design collect, protect, analyze
stages.detail: Three systems, three distinct jobs: SBD-SYSLOG01 gathers, SBD-AUDIT01 preserves, SBD-SPLUNK01 answers questions. Decide what is collected first, how long it lives, and who may touch which stage — before a single event flows.

stages.title: Turn on the right auditing
stages.detail: Forwarding garbage faster is not monitoring. Set the advanced audit policy so the events that tell the network's story — sign-ins, account changes, directory changes, policy changes — actually get written.

stages.title: Build the collector
stages.detail: SBD-SYSLOG01 becomes the funnel: Windows Event Forwarding brings the DC and admin-host events in by subscription, and the core router's denies arrive as syslog — one host where the network's record first lands.

stages.title: Protect the record on SBD-AUDIT01
stages.detail: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: scheduled archives from the collector, hashed on arrival, readable by few, deletable by process only.

stages.title: Analyze in SBD-SPLUNK01
stages.detail: Analysis earns its place with three working searches and one alert: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself.

stages.title: Prove the chain and delta scan
stages.detail: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the repository's next archive, and the analyst's screen — then the cadence scans close the course.

courses.outcomeSummary: Every important event collected, protected from tampering, and answering a search someone actually runs.

courses.title: Bring in the fleet
courses.subtitle: 50 Windows endpoints, managed from first boot
courses.description: Join the fifty-workstation fleet to a network that is ready for it: DHCP addressing, OU landing with STIG policy at first boot, Windows LAPS for every local administrator, certificate autoenrollment at scale, and a sampled proof with the whole rollout observed by the logging pipeline.
outcomes: Roll fifty endpoints in waves that land hardened, addressed, and registered untouched.
Manage every local administrator with Windows LAPS under the tier model.
Prove the fleet with a defined sample, a failure rule, and pipeline-observed joins.

stages.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
stages.detail: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.

stages.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
stages.detail: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.

stages.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
stages.detail: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.

stages.title: Autoenroll the fleet's certificates
stages.detail: Course 1.4 proved autoenrollment on a pilot group; this lesson turns it loose. Widen the template permission to the fleet, let policy do the enrolling, and verify a machine certificate chains and checks revocation across the boundary.

stages.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
stages.detail: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.

stages.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
stages.detail: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.

stages.title: Delta scan the fleet and hand off
stages.detail: The cadence meets its first population: Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) baselines on the sampled endpoints with the Windows client benchmark, rescans where the course changed infrastructure, and a fleet inventory that course 1.8's tooling will take over.

courses.outcomeSummary: Fifty endpoints that arrive hardened, certified, and watched from their very first sign-in.

courses.title: Patch, protect, and watch for weakness
courses.subtitle: WSUS rings, approved sources, ePO & credentialed scanning
courses.description: Keep the proven state from drifting: Windows updates through WSUS rings fed across the air gap, one approved source per software type with SBD-REPO01 for packages, a living inventory on SBD-MGMT01, managed endpoint protection through SBD-EPO01, and SBD-NESSUS01 turning the scan cadence into routine.
outcomes: Deliver updates and software through ring-gated, single-source, air-gap-fed channels.
Prove protection coverage against a living component inventory.
Run credentialed vulnerability scanning on the standing cadence with classified findings.

stages.title: Design the rings and the software rules
stages.detail: Decide how change reaches the network before any of it does: update rings that try things on the expendable before the essential, one approved source per software type, and register rows for every new path.

stages.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 and the ring policies
stages.detail: WSUS becomes the only road Windows updates travel: content imported across the air gap, approvals per ring, and Group Policy objects (GPOs) that point every OU at the server — with a pilot ring that proves each approval first.

stages.title: Build SBD-REPO01 for approved packages
stages.detail: The lab's Linux hosts and tooling need packages, and the rule from lesson 1 applies to them too: one internal repository, fed across the boundary, serving only what was reviewed in.

stages.title: SBD-MGMT01 and the living inventory
stages.detail: The course 1.7 fleet inventory was a snapshot; SBD-MGMT01 makes it a living record — every system, its ring, its sources, its last-seen state — maintained from the management seat the model placed in VLAN 70.

stages.title: Endpoint protection through SBD-EPO01
stages.detail: Protection becomes a managed fact, not fifty local settings: the ePO server deploys agents ring by ring, policy comes from one console, and the fleet's protection state is something the dashboard can simply show.

stages.title: SBD-NESSUS01 and the standing cadence
stages.detail: The course 1.3 cadence grows its instrument: credentialed scans per VLAN on schedule, findings flowing into the pipeline and the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) habit, and this course's five new systems getting their own baselines on the way out.

courses.outcomeSummary: Updates by ring, software from approved sources, managed protection, and a scanner that keeps everyone honest.

courses.title: Stand up the business services
courses.subtitle: Files, database, licensing & web — by documented paths
courses.description: Give the users what the network exists for: SBD-FS01's role-based shares over verified SMB security, SBD-WEB01 serving internal HTTPS from a hardened, domain-joined Linux Apache, SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API, and SBD-SQL01 running as a managed identity behind exactly one caller — every hop a documented, proven register row.
outcomes: Serve files through role-group permissions with verified SMB signing and encryption.
Run the database as a managed identity, certificate-encrypted, with SBD-APPS01 as its only caller.
Prove the fleet → web → application → database chain with every hop registered and every shortcut denied.

stages.title: Design the service paths and identities
stages.detail: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.

stages.title: Build SBD-FS01 with least-privilege shares
stages.detail: The file server is where access control meets daily life. Build the shares against the role groups, require SMB signing on the server instead of trusting client defaults, and make 'who can read this' a one-lookup question.

stages.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
stages.detail: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.

stages.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
stages.detail: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.

stages.title: Reconcile, scan, and hand off
stages.detail: The business services close the way every build course has: the register reconciled against live behavior, the new systems baselined, the inventory updated — and for the first time, the network is functionally complete.

courses.outcomeSummary: Files, licensing, and a three-tier web application, each reachable only by its documented path.

courses.title: Prove you can recover
courses.subtitle: Backups with custody, one rehearsed restore & the closing record
courses.description: Close the Build path by proving the network can come back: scheduled directory and CA backups under ceremony-grade custody, policy, boundary, logs, and the living records in one hashed catalog, a timed restore rehearsal in isolation, and the recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence.
outcomes: Back up the directory, CA, policy, boundary, logs, and records into one verified catalog.
Rehearse a real system state restore in isolation, measured against written objectives.
File the tested-recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence for path 2.

stages.title: Decide what recovery must prove
stages.detail: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.

stages.title: Back up the directory, on schedule
stages.detail: System state from both controllers, on a schedule, to the protected target — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.

stages.title: Back up the CA, policy, boundary, and records
stages.detail: The directory is not the only thing the network cannot re-derive: the issuing CA's database and key, the Group Policy set, the router's configuration, the log archive, and the living records each get their protected, cataloged copy.

stages.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
stages.detail: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.

stages.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
stages.detail: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.

stages.title: File the recovery record and close the path
stages.detail: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the final scans snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.

courses.outcomeSummary: Backups with custody, one real restore performed in isolation, and the evidence that you can come back.

categories.title: Build the Network
categories.description: Build the complete air-gapped network, one course at a time: identity, DNS and time, a hardened baseline, the two-tier PKI, tiered administration, logging, the workstation fleet, patching and scanning, business services, and proven recovery. Follow the courses in order, from 1.1 to 1.10.

categories.title: Network Authorization
categories.description: Prepare the network’s Body of Evidence and Authorization to Operate package. Start after the network build, with course 2.1.
